Lisianthus is used because it is the name NC State's description gives the plant. RHS lists Eustoma russellianum as a synonym. records.name_note: Sources differ in how they lead: NC State's page for this exact species (H1 'Momordica charantia') carries a Common Name(s) list, alphabetized and in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, of Ampalaya, Balsam Pear, Bitter Gourd, Bitter Melon, and its description text calls the plant 'Bitter Goard'; UF/IFAS HS1271, a dedicated page for this species, has the H1 'Bitter Melon—an Asian Vegetable Expanding in Florida' and lists bitter gourd, bitter squash, Goya melon, karela and balsam pear as other names. 'Bitter Melon' is chosen because the UF/IFAS page leads with it; it is the fourth entry of NC State's list, whose first entry is Ampalaya.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox, Poison block (human-scoped; this is the page's 'Poisonous to Humans' block, separate from any cat/dog tags, and the page carries no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag): Poison Severity: Medium. Poison Symptoms: 'TOXIC ONLY IF LARGE QUANTITIES EATEN. Ripe fruits, fruit coats, and seeds cause headache, salivation, facial redness, pupil dilation, stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and muscular weakness.' Poison Toxic Principle: Resin, saponic glycoside, and alkaloids. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Fruits, Seeds. Page Plant Type values as rendered: Annual, Edible, Poisonous, Vine. Page Problems field: Malodorous, Poisonous to Humans, Weedy. Page tags: #poisonous #edible garden #vine #annual #annual vine #orange fruits #yellow flowers #spreading #tendrils #herbaceous vine. Page prose: 'The mature fruit and seeds are toxic and should not be eaten.' Fruit Description: 'Edible when still green, but poisonous once ripe.' Edibility (conditional): 'Young fruits (green or early yellow colored) are a popular vegetable consumed in some countries. Leafy shoot tips are often used as salad greens.' So young green or early-yellow fruits and leafy shoot tips are eaten; never ripe fruit or seeds. No cat or dog toxicity statement was found on an admissible source, so toxic_to_pets is left null. Scope note: UF/IFAS HS1271 says harvested fruit is 'green or slightly yellow', that the seeds are removed and discarded, and (in a figure caption) that immature seeds have 'edible arils'; NC State says the seeds are toxic, so the admissible sources differ somewhat on whether any seed tissue is edible. Treat seeds as not to be eaten.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source names cats or dogs; NC State's poison block is human-scoped (and the page has no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag).

Edibility is conditional: NC State says young fruits (green or early yellow colored) are a popular vegetable and leafy shoot tips are often used as salad greens, but ripe fruits, fruit coats and seeds are poisonous. UF/IFAS HS1271 also says the fruit is harvested green or slightly yellow with seeds removed and discarded, yet its figure caption mentions edible arils on immature seeds; sources differ on seed tissue. Do not treat ripe fruit or seeds as food.

NC State's Dimensions block gives Height 12-20 ft; its description frames this as the length the vine grows in one season (plant itself 4 to 6 inches high), so mature_height_in is vine length, not a free-standing height. UF/IFAS says the species "grows vines up to 16 feet long with many branches" and that "The trellis system is usually 6 feet high."

(a survival statement, not a damage-onset temperature); UF/IFAS gives 60-95 F only for seed germination soil. records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Levisticum officinale page has the bare binomial as its H1. Its rendered Common Name(s) list is Bladder seed, Garden Lovage, Lovage, Maggi plant, in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, so Bladder seed is first and Lovage third. Lovage is used as common_name because it is the name the description uses: the Description opens 'Lovage is a flowering, herbaceous perennial in the carrot family' and uses Lovage throughout. NC State lists Hipposelinum levisticum and Levisticum paludapifolium as previously known names. This is a different taxon from Apium graveolens (Celery), whose NC State Common Name(s) list is Celery, Smallage, Wild Celery. The Lovage page says its flowers taste like celery and its deeply divided leaves resemble parsley or celery leaves.
records.toxicity_detail: All from NC State's Levisticum officinale page. The page's top line says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Its "Poisonous to Humans" block (human-scoped) gives Poison Severity Low, Poison Symptoms "Diuretic, increased urination", Poison Toxic Principle "Volatile oils, especially phthalide lactones.", and Causes Contact Dermatitis "No". The page names no specific poisonous plant part, no handling warning and no dose or preparation instruction for the poison. Separately from that human block, the page's Problems field and its Tags carry "Problem for Cats", "Problem for Dogs" and "Problem for Horses". The page carries no symptom list, severity or toxic principle for those animals. The full tag list is: #problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats #herb garden #edible #edible leaves #edible fruits #herbaceous perennial #herb #edible roots #edible flowers #ornamentals #culinary #rhizomatous. The Plant Type values are Edible, Herb and Herbaceous Perennial. The Edibility field says: "All parts are edible; seeds and leaves as flavoring, root as a vegetable, and flowers in soups and salads." The same page therefore lists the plant as edible and as a cat and dog problem. No other admissible source was read, so there is nothing to compare for scope.

The Clemson page returned HTTP 403, MoBot plantfinder was blocked by the sandbox, and the RHS URLs tried did not yield a dedicated Levisticum officinale plant page. records.name_note: Sources split on the lead name. RHS's dedicated page renders 'chaste tree' as its plant-profile subtitle beneath the binomial H1 (page title 'Vitex agnus-castus | chaste tree') and separately lists hemp tree, monk's pepper, Queensland lignum-vitae and tree of chastity as other common names. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list, in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, lists Chasteberry first, then Chastetree, Chaste Tree, Lilac Chastetree, Monk's Pepper, Texas Lilac, and its Description opens 'The chaste tree is a shrub or tree native to Europe, western Asia, India and North Africa.' Chaste Tree was chosen because it leads on RHS, opens NC State's description, and is also an entry in NC State's list.
unknowns: Only NC State and RHS had readable dedicated pages. MoBot's Plant Finder page failed to load (connection/certificate error in the sandbox), UF/IFAS's chastetree publication (ST664) returns HTTP 410 as retired, Clemson HGIC's chastetree factsheet returns HTTP 403, and the UGA Field Report chaste tree item is a PDF the page-text extractor cannot read. Penn State and UGA results were multi-species articles and were not used.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: neither admissible page read carries a Poison block, a Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag or any toxicity statement for this plant. NC State's Ethnobotany line (essential oils in fruits and leaves, used as an insect repellent) and its fruit description (purple, pungent flavor) are not safety claims. Absence of a record is not evidence of safety.

is_edible left null: no readable admissible page says the fruit (chasteberry) or any part is grown or used for food. Herbal or medicinal chasteberry use is not stated on NC State or RHS and is not captured.

water_regime left null: neither page gives a watering statement. NC State's Drought and Dry Soil resistance tags and 'good drought tolerance once established' are tolerance traits, and RHS 'Drought Resistance Yes' likewise. RHS Moisture 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained' is a soil moisture field and was used only for soil_drainage.

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), whose Acid and Alkaline bands are open-ended, and RHS lists pH Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so no ceiling or floor is supported.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figure is the generic NC State light-category legend wording, not species-specific prose.
chill_damage_f left null: NC State gives hardiness zones 7a-8b and notes winter dieback in USDA Zones 5 and 6, and RHS rates it H4; these are survival ratings, not a damage-onset temperature.

NC State's species Dimensions block reads Height: 8 ft. 0 in. - 20 ft. 0 in. and Width: 5 ft. 0 in. - 20 ft. 0 in.; its prose says "Although typically grown as a 10- to 15-foot shrub, in tree form it can reach heights and widths of up to 20 feet." Cultivars range from 3-6 ft to 25-30 ft. RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread of 1.5-2.5 metres (UK conditions), not used.

soil_base garden_bed reflects in-ground culture (NC State Soil Texture clay, loam, sand; RHS Soil Types Chalk, Loam, Sand); no source frames it as a container plant. is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field is Shrub / Tree with USDA zones 7a-8b, and RHS describes a deciduous shrub for a sheltered, sunny site.

NC State flags the plant as weedy and potentially invasive ('freely reseeds and can become weedy'; 'potential to become invasive, especially in southern areas of the country'); cultivar sizes vary widely.
